title: An organic semiconductor-based photocatalyst sheet for overall solar-driven water splitting - Nature Energy
text:
Download PDF

AbstractSplitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using sunlight offers a route to renewable fuel, but translating this reaction into systems suitable for industrial implementation remains difficult. Photocatalyst sheets can overcome key limitations of common direct water-splitting approaches (photoelectrochemical devices and photocatalyst dispersions), but existing photocatalyst sheets rely on inorganic semiconductor nanoparticles and processing techniques that can be difficult to scale. Here we show that solution-processed organic semiconductors can form water-splitting photocatalyst sheets by simply tailoring the charge extraction layer beneath the light-absorbing film. A single organic semiconductor active layer (deposited as a bulk heterojunction blend) drives either hydrogen or oxygen evolution depending on its underlying molecular contact, yielding photocathode and photoanode half-cells with well-matched photocurrents. Combining both reactions on one substrate using a microdomain-patterned molecular underlayer affords a photocatalyst sheet that achieves unassisted water splitting under simulated sunlight for over 2 h and generates hydrogen at a stabilized rate of 1.3 µmol h−1 cm−2, which corresponds to a solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 0.1%.

Organic Photovoltaic Technology and Performance

MainSolar-driven hydrogen (H2) production via overall water splitting (OWS) is a promising route towards renewable fuels and chemical feedstocks at a scale commensurate with current energy demands1. The most established technology enabling this process, photovoltaic-coupled electrochemistry (PV-EC), is already available2. However, its high cost and complex device configuration limit its competitiveness with fossil fuel-derived H2 (ref. 3). By contrast, artificial photosynthesis in the form of ‘Z-scheme’ photoelectrochemical (PEC)4 and heterogeneous photocatalytic5 systems offers simpler architectures and heat integration benefits6 by directly consolidating light-harvesting and fuel production into semiconductor/liquid junctions while also employing two light-harvesting systems (the H2 evolution reaction (HER) and O2 evolution reaction (OER)) to increase solar utilization relative to single semiconductor systems7,8.The great potential of Z-scheme PEC and photocatalytic water splitting has driven intensive research over recent decades. However, both approaches face inherent challenges. In PEC systems where a semiconductor photocathode and photoanode, respectively, drive the HER and OER, ohmic losses and ion transport complicate large-area implementation, while the requisite multi-electrode configuration and external circuit increase module cost and limit scalability. Heterogeneous photocatalytic systems, comprising separate H2- and O2-evolving particles dispersed in water, suffer from colloidal stability limitations while also relying on dissolved redox mediators to shuttle charges between the components9,10,11,12,13. These redox mediators cause parasitic light absorption, while inherent charge back-transfer also substantially reduces the solar-to-hydrogen (STH) conversion efficiency14.To address the key challenges of the Z-scheme PEC and photocatalytic approaches, a ‘photocatalyst sheet’ concept has been recently proposed. The prototypical photocatalyst sheet consists of H2- and O2-evolving particles deposited side by side onto an electrically conductive substrate, enabling direct electron shuttling and avoiding colloidal instability issues. Domen and co-workers proposed a photocatalyst sheet using La,Rh-doped SrTiO3 and Mo-doped BiVO4 as the H2- and O2-evolving particles, respectively. These were deposited onto gold, achieving 1.1% STH conversion efficiency15. Compared with conventional PEC cells, photocatalyst sheets offer higher scalability16,17, lower ohmic resistance and reduced mass-transport limitations by eliminating external wiring and decreasing the distance between the H2 and O2 evolution domains18. To date, various conductive substrates, such as gold15,19, carbon18 or F-doped SnO2 (FTO)20, and inorganic semiconductor nanoparticle-based light absorbers like SrTiO3 (refs. 15,18), Cu2O (ref. 20), LaMg1/3Ta2/3O2N (ref. 19) and BiVO4 (refs. 15,18,19,20) have been employed in photocatalyst sheets for OWS. However, inorganic semiconductors often suffer from intrinsic drawbacks, including large bandgaps, fixed band edge positions and high-temperature (energy-intensive) synthesis21. In addition, translating inorganic nanoparticle-based Z-scheme photocatalytic systems from dispersion into the desired final photocatalyst sheet architecture typically requires complicated and labour-intensive techniques, such as particle-transfer methods15,18,19. Therefore, identifying semiconductor materials that are effective at light-harvesting, tunable and scalable, as well as developing rational strategies to construct photocatalyst sheets, remain critical challenges in this field.To this end, organic semiconductors (OSs), consisting of π-conjugated carbon-based building blocks, are promising candidates due to their superior light absorption ability, solution processability and structural tunability22. In particular, their accessibility to chemical modification at the molecular level allows precise control over their optoelectronic properties22. This advantage of OSs has served as a basis for their use in various electronic applications, such as organic photovoltaics23,24,25,26 and photodetectors27,28,29. Recently, the bulk heterojunction (BHJ) strategy, which employs an OS donor and acceptor blend to substantially enhance photogenerated charge separation, has been translated to PEC (refs. 30,31,32,33,34,35) and nanoparticle photocatalytic36,37,38,39,40,41,42 water-splitting systems, yielding promising results. However, despite the advantages of OSs and their proven capability to drive OWS, an OS-based photocatalyst sheet has not yet been realized.In this Article, we report the capability of a single OS BHJ to facilitate either the HER or OER through molecular underlayer engineering. Leveraging this advance, we establish a concept for a scalable OS-based photocatalyst sheet, using the BHJ coupled with a microdomain substrate architecture and suitable co-catalysts, that demonstrates OWS operation under standard testing conditions.Molecular underlayers switch BHJ photoelectrode polarityWhile most conventional inorganic semiconductor-based photocatalyst sheets have been inspired by heterogeneous nanoparticle-based photocatalytic systems employing separate semiconductors for the H2- and O2-evolving particles15,18,19, we hypothesized that a single BHJ OS layer with suitable energy levels, when integrated with the appropriate charge-selective underlayers and co-catalysts, could be capable of driving either the HER or the OER. The step-by-step development of this concept towards a scalable OS-based photocatalyst sheet concept is presented schematically in Fig. 1. Establishing OWS using a side-by-side photoanode/photocathode PEC system (Fig. 1a) represents the first step. Translating the system onto a single substrate in an integrated parallel cell (Fig. 1b) represents an intermediate step towards the final photocatalyst sheet device (Fig. 1c), wherein underlayer microdomains are employed to define HER and OER regions, and charges are shuttled between domains via the transparent conductive substrate (for example FTO) to enable wireless and unbiased OWS.Fig. 1: Development process of the OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheet.Full size imagea, The first design step representing the photocathode/photoanode side-by-side PEC cell using a single BHJ on an FTO substrate modified with an appropriate hole-selective contact (HSC) and electron-selective contact (ESC). b, Integration of the photoanode and photocathode onto a single FTO substrate, as an intermediate parallel design. c, The final, scalable photocatalyst (PC) sheet concept using microdomain patterning of the HSC and ESC. The dashed yellow lines mark the boundaries between the HER and OER domains. The schematics here represent simplified device structures for better visualization of the development process.To realize this concept, we chose an OS-based BHJ active layer suitable for both the HER and OER. A polymer donor PBDTTTPD and polymer acceptor PNDIHDT (see chemical structures in Fig. 2a) were selected based on the appropriate energy level alignment between their highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMOs) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMOs), relative to the HER and OER potentials34 (Fig. 2b). Moreover, the two polymers absorb light complementarily in the range between 300 and 500 nm (Supplementary Fig. 1) and are mechanically robust43,44. This has enabled their impressive performance in photovoltaics45 and photocathodes33,34.Fig. 2: Control of the OS BHJ-based PEC device behaviour by CSC engineering.Full size imagea, Chemical structures of OS materials used for the BHJ. b, Energy levels of the BHJ34 aligned with the work function of FTO shifted by molecular functionalization, and HER and OER potentials at pH 9 versus the vacuum energy (Evac) and normal hydrogen electrode (ENHE). c, Chemical structures of 2PACz and NI-PA molecules together with their molecular dipole moments. d, Schematics of the individual PEC devices for sacrificial oxidation and reduction reactions. e,f, LSV curves of devices under intermittent simulated 1-sun illumination for sacrificial persulfate reduction (e) and sulfite oxidation (f), at pH 9. The light source used in this study was calibrated to deliver a photon flux equivalent to the standard solar spectrum (ASTM G173-03) across the absorption range of the BHJ film (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 5).To verify that the PBDTTTPD:PNDIHDT blend (hereafter called BHJ) is capable of driving both the HER and OER via underlayer engineering, we modified the FTO substrate surface with charge-selective contact (CSC) molecules, namely, (2-(9H-carbazol-9-yl)ethyl)phosphonic acid (2PACz) and (2-(1,3-dioxo-1H-benzo[de]isoquinolin-2(3H)-yl)ethyl)phosphonic acid (NI-PA) (Fig. 2c). The synthesis of NI-PA is described in Methods and was confirmed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 2). The phosphonic acid groups on these molecules serve as substrate anchors while the carbazole and naphthalene imide moieties of 2PACz and NI-PA, respectively, induce molecular dipole moments of opposite direction (calculated by density functional theory (DFT), Supplementary Figs. 3a and 4a), as indicated in Fig. 2c. The dipoles modulate the work function of the FTO (as measured by ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS), Supplementary Figs. 3b,c and 4b,c), imposing a preferential charge extraction from the BHJ (Fig. 2b), where 2PACz and NI-PA are expected to function as a (p-type) hole-selective contact (HSC) and an (n-type) electron-selective contact (ESC), respectively.To demonstrate control over PEC behaviour using the molecular underlayers, we fabricated photoelectrodes with an FTO/(HSC-or-ESC)/BHJ structure (schematic illustrations are presented in Fig. 2d) and performed linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) under sacrificial conditions (that is, either persulfate reduction or sulfite oxidation) at pH 9 with intermittent simulated 1-sun illumination. Fabrication procedures for these devices are detailed in Methods and a BHJ thickness optimization is described in Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 6.The FTO/2PACz/BHJ photoelectrode exhibits photo-driven persulfate reduction with a photocurrent density magnitude (Jph) of 2.6 mA cm−2 at 0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE), while showing negligible Jph for sulfite oxidation, as shown in Fig. 2e and Fig. 2f, respectively. Conversely, the FTO/NI-PA/BHJ photoelectrode reaches a Jph of 3.5 mA cm−2 at 1.23 VRHE under sacrificial photo-oxidation conditions but exhibits substantially smaller Jph for persulfate reduction. Omitting underlayers in a control device (FTO/BHJ) leads to very small Jph values for both sacrificial reactions. These results indicate that the molecular underlayers facilitate preferential extraction of one charge carrier type, although passing the disfavoured charge carrier through these molecular layers is possible with sufficient applied bias (see the schematic in Supplementary Fig. 7), as evidenced by the small Jph value of the NI-PA-based device for persulfate reduction at 0 VRHE. Additionally, the critical role of the BHJ in free charge generation, compared to single-polymer films, is described in Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. 8.Remarkably, we found the CSC-based switching effect with 2PACz/NI-PA to function with another BHJ, as described in Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10, suggesting generalizability and elucidating the importance of underlayer engineering in tuning the BHJ photoelectrode operation. Switching the response between photocathode and photoanode by simply changing the underlayer suggests that a single BHJ could drive both the HER and OER.To demonstrate this, we fabricated individual photoelectrodes with co-catalyst overlayers. Specifically, photocathodes for the HER were prepared by photo-assisted electrodeposition of Pt onto FTO/2PACz/BHJ (Supplementary Fig. 11). To fabricate photoanodes for the OER, layers of poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] (PTAA) and amorphous Li-IrOx (LIO) nanoparticles were sequentially spray-coated onto FTO/NI-PA/BHJ devices as a hole-transport layer and OER co-catalyst, respectively. The PTAA layer is essential for stable OER operation to avoid hole accumulation in the BHJ33. The morphology of the PTAA and LIO nanoparticles is shown in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images in Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13, respectively. Top-view SEM images of the PTAA and LIO layers on the BHJ photoanode are shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. The optimization of catalyst amounts deposited on the photoelectrodes is discussed in Supplementary Note 5 (Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16).It is important to note a critical design consideration in anticipation of the final photocatalyst sheet concept (Fig. 1c). While the photo-driven reduction of the Pt will localize the HER co-catalyst to photocathode regions, the PTAA and LIO OER co-catalyst will be deposited uniformly over the entire device. Accordingly, we employed nanoparticles for both PTAA and LIO to afford porous overlayer structures to facilitate water ingress and ensure direct contact with the Pt co-catalyst for water reduction. The individual photoelectrode structures for the HER and OER are shown in Fig. 3a.Fig. 3: Development of individual photoelectrodes for the HER and OER.Full size imagea, Schematics of the photocathode (left) and photoanode (right) devices. b, LSV curves from PEC measurements of the individual photoelectrodes under intermittent simulated 1-sun illumination in NaBi buffer electrolyte (pH 9).The LSV curves under intermittent illumination from the two individual devices, both tested in pH 9 sodium borate (NaBi) electrolyte, are shown in Fig. 3b. The photocathode has a photocurrent onset around 0.98 VRHE and a Jph of 4.1 mA cm−2 at 0 VRHE (extended scan range presented in Supplementary Fig. 17). The photocurrent onset of the photoanode is around 0.35 VRHE and Jph reaches 2.7 mA cm−2 at 1.23 VRHE. Analogous testing with a second BHJ shows a similar behaviour (Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Fig. 18). We note that, in both cases the photocurrents for the HER and OER exhibit sufficient overlap within the potential range from 0.4 to 0.8 VRHE, implying that an unbiased wired PEC cell or photocatalyst sheet can perform solar-driven OWS with these device configurations.Chronoamperometry (CA) measurements were performed to verify this. The individual photocathode and the photoanode retain measurable performance after 30 min of continuous operation at 0 and 1.23 VRHE, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 19), and when tested together in a side-by-side wired configuration (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20) under uniform simulated 1-sun illumination, an unbiased initial photocurrent of over 0.5 mA cm−2 was observed. While the photocurrent decreased under continuous operation, the device remained active after 2 h. Based on the measured Jph after 30 min of stabilization, the estimated STH conversion efficiency was calculated to be 0.12%.Wireless integration of half-cells onto a single substrateTo integrate the wired side-by-side PEC cells onto one substrate with a continuous BHJ layer, a wireless ‘parallel photocatalyst sheet’ was developed, where one half of an FTO substrate was functionalized with 2PACz and the other half with NI-PA to define the HER and OER domains, respectively (Fig. 4). While this geometry is not amenable to large-scale implementation due to the ohmic resistance of the FTO, at small scale this limitation is minimized, and demonstrating operation in this configuration represents an important intermediate step.Fig. 4: Intermediate, parallel-type (half-half design) photocatalyst sheet.Full size imagea, Schematic of the integrated parallel photocatalyst sheet architecture. b, LSV curve from PEC measurement in NaBi electrolyte (pH 9) under intermittent simulated 1-sun illumination. c, H2 and O2 production rates over time of the parallel photocatalyst sheet measured by GC during bias-free solar-driven OWS operation under continuous simulated 1-sun illumination. The inset shows the ratio of produced H2 to O2.The fabrication steps to assemble this structure are described in Supplementary Fig. 21 and Methods. The segregated CSC layer deposition was confirmed by Kelvin-probe force microscopy (KPFM). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 22, the FTO/2PACz region exhibits a reduced contact potential difference (CPD) of 1 mV, whereas the FTO/NI-PA region shows an elevated CPD of 482 mV. Both are distinct from bare FTO (151 mV) and a film deposited from an equimolar mix of both molecules (99 mV). The subsequent deposition of the BHJ, followed by the photo-assisted electrodeposition of Pt and the uniform spray deposition of the PTAA and LIO nanoparticles over the entire device area, completed the fabrication of the parallel photocatalyst sheet (Fig. 4a). We note that the Pt co-catalyst is selectively deposited onto the FTO/2PACz region as the NI-PA underlayer suppresses the PEC reduction of Pt under the employed conditions. Supplementary Fig. 23 supports this by showing the electrical charge passed during Pt deposition on both FTO/2PACz/BHJ and FTO/NI-PA/BHJ, together with photographs and top-view SEM images of parallel devices showing the selective deposition of Pt onto the 2PACz region.We performed LSV measurements in NaBi electrolyte at pH 9 with the parallel photocatalyst sheet, uniformly illuminating both HER and OER areas. The device shows the expected ambipolar behaviour resulting from the overall sum current density (J) of the two domains (Fig. 4b). In detail, the photocathode domain dominates at low applied bias, leading to an overall cathodic photocurrent. As the applied bias increases, the photoanodic behaviour becomes more pronounced, resulting in a decrease of the overall photocurrent, eventually crossing zero at 0.64 VRHE. The current crossover potential is consistent with the point where the individual photoelectrodes produce equal but opposite Jph values. Thus, at this potential both domains generate equal photocurrent magnitudes and electrons are shuttled from the OER to the HER domain exclusively through the FTO substrate.Next, the parallel photocatalyst sheet was examined for unassisted solar-driven water splitting under continuous simulated 1-sun illumination by placing it inside a 20 ml purge-type photocatalyst reactor vial containing NaBi (pH 9) electrolyte (Supplementary Fig. 24), directly connected to a gas chromatograph (GC) to analyse H2 and O2 production. Figure 4c shows the detected H2 and O2 production rates of the parallel photocatalyst sheet over time. After 30 min of stabilization under continuous simulated 1-sun illumination, the system produced around 1.8 μmol h−1 cm−2 of H2. Importantly, the ratio of the produced H2 to O2 was 2 (see inset of Fig. 4c), which confirms OWS. The stabilized H2 production rate corresponds to an estimated STH conversion efficiency of 0.12%, which is comparable to the value estimated from the Jph value of the wired side-by-side PEC device (Supplementary Fig. 19).For comparison, the single photoelectrodes (Fig. 3) were examined under bias-free testing conditions as controls (Supplementary Fig. 25) and neither individual photoelectrode produced detectable amounts of H2 or O2 when operated as photocatalyst sheets. This further highlights the need to integrate designated domains for both half-reactions into a rationally designed photocatalyst sheet for OWS.Fabrication of scalable microdomain photocatalyst sheetsDespite the successful demonstration of the performance of the half-half parallel photocatalyst sheet, as mentioned previously, this device architecture has limited scalability due to ohmic losses in the substrate and mass-transport limitations in the electrolyte. Indeed, diffusion-based mass-transport models suggest that the ideal domain size is in the millimetre to micrometre range depending on the tolerable losses46,47,48. To investigate the effect of domain size on the device performance, we employed a contact printing49 approach using polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamps to afford precise control over the CSC layer domain sizes. PDMS stamps with differently sized cylindrical features (Supplementary Fig. 26) were coated with 2PACz solution, dried and pressed onto activated FTO substrates. This was followed by deposition of NI-PA onto the unfunctionalized substrate areas using a simple impregnation technique (Fig. 5a). Figure 5b shows the KPFM surface potential map of an underlayer film prepared using a PDMS stamp with 10-μm-diameter features. The isolated circular areas correspond to the stamp features and show a reduced CPD, indicating successful 2PACz functionalization, whereas the continuous area has a higher CPD due to the deposition of NI-PA. Similar domain-dependent CPD shifts were found for patterned underlayer films prepared using 1,000-μm- and 100-μm-diameter feature-size stamps (Supplementary Fig. 27). Meanwhile, the surface roughness remained homogeneous over the entire sample area, as seen from the corresponding topography maps in Supplementary Fig. 28.Fig. 5: Micropatterning of CSC underlayers with PDMS stamps.Full size imagea, Schematic illustration of the preparation process of the microdomain surface functionalization layer using PDMS stamps. b, KPFM surface potential map of the microdomain surface-functionalization layer on FTO deposited using a 10-μm-feature size PDMS stamp for 2PACz deposition, followed by deposition of NI-PA. The colour scale varies linearly between the indicated end values. c–e, Top-view SEM images of Pt domains deposited by photo-assisted electrodeposition on top of BHJ layers on 1,000-μm-domain (c), 100-μm-domain (d) and 10-μm-domain (e) CSC underlayers.Fabrication of the microdomain photocatalyst sheets proceeded by spin-coating the BHJ on the patterned substrate followed by Pt HER co-catalyst deposition by photo-electroreduction. The Pt deposition on the BHJ selectively over the 2PACz microdomains is clearly seen in the top-view SEM images (Fig. 5c‒e), illustrating that the effect of the underlayer microdomains persists through the BHJ films. The influence of BHJ film thickness on underlayer domain persistence is discussed in Supplementary Note 7 and Supplementary Fig. 29.Following the Pt deposition, PTAA and LIO nanoparticles were added uniformly over the substrate to complete the device. Figure 6a shows a schematic illustration of the final device structure. The optimization of co-catalyst amounts deposited on the microdomain devices is discussed in Supplementary Note 8 and Supplementary Fig. 30. LSV data of a 1,000-µm-domain photocatalyst sheet in Fig. 6b show a similar behaviour to that of the half-half parallel cell, where photocathodic and photoanodic responses are evident at low and high applied potentials, respectively. There is a crossover potential at 0.56 VRHE, which is slightly shifted compared to the half-half device. The LSV curves of devices based on 100 µm and 10 µm domains (Supplementary Fig. 31) show comparable responses.Fig. 6: Microdomain underlayer OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheet.Full size imagea, Schematic of the device architecture. b, LSV curve from PEC measurements of the 1,000-μm-domain OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheet in NaBi electrolyte (pH 9) under intermittent simulated 1-sun illumination. c, H2 and O2 production rates over time of the unassisted 1,000-μm-domain photocatalyst sheet measured by GC during solar-driven OWS operation under continuous simulated 1-sun illumination. The inset shows the ratio of produced H2 to O2. d, OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheet device STH conversion efficiency as a function of domain size, in comparison with the parallel cell. Tested domain sizes were 1,000 µm, 100 µm and 10 µm. The average STH conversion efficiency and standard deviation (error bars) were calculated from independent devices, with n = 3 for the parallel cell and n = 5, 4 and 3 for domain sizes of 1,000 µm, 100 µm and 10 µm, respectively. The red and blue regions represent the parallel and microdomain CSC architectures of the photocatalyst sheet, respectively.Finally, the BHJ-based microdomain photocatalyst sheets were examined for unassisted solar-driven water splitting under identical experimental conditions to the parallel photocatalyst sheet. Figure 6c shows the detected H2 and O2 production rates of the 1,000-μm-domain OS photocatalyst sheet over time. Initially, the system produced more than 1.6 μmol h−1 cm−2 of H2 under simulated 1-sun illumination. Importantly, after 30 min stabilization, the ratio of produced H2 to O2 corresponds to the expected value of 2 (inset in Fig. 6c), at a H2 production rate of 1.3 μmol h−1 cm−2. The average STH conversion efficiency, obtained from multiple independently fabricated devices, is estimated to be 0.1%, which is comparable to that of the parallel cell. The higher H2-to-O2 ratio observed at the start of the photocatalyst sheet operation is likely to be due to initial oxidation of slightly reduced co-catalyst layers50. The production rates slowly decrease under continuous operation, still producing 0.72 μmol h−1 cm−2 of H2 after 120 min.Similarly, the OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheets constructed with the 100- and 10-μm-domain underlayers were tested for unbiased solar-driven OWS. As summarized in Fig. 6d, the photocatalyst sheets with smaller domain sizes exhibit considerably lower performance than the parallel cell and 1,000-μm-domain photocatalyst sheet. This performance loss is attributed to slower charge extraction in the BHJ at the boundaries between 2PACz and NI-PA microdomains, which increases the fraction of charges that recombine before extraction as the domain size decreases (detailed discussion is provided in Supplementary Note 9). While these results indicate a trade off between domain size miniaturization and effective charge extraction in our BHJ photocatalyst sheet design, it is noteworthy that the 1,000 µm domain size remains in the range where minimal mass-transport losses are expected under the conditions tested even at much higher H2 production rates47, thereby supporting feasibility towards scale-up.While the use of PDMS stamps allows for precise area control when depositing the microdomain underlayer, a more scalable and broadly accessible method for patterning the underlayer would be useful for large-scale implementation. Accordingly, we developed a spray-deposition method for microdomain underlayer formation as a final demonstration of our photocatalyst sheet concept (Supplementary Discussion). Using an ultrasonic spray system, a stochastic arrangement of 2PACz microdomains on FTO was realized and subsequently surrounded by NI-PA deposited by impregnation (Supplementary Fig. 32). The resulting underlayer molecular surface modification distribution was imaged by KPFM (Supplementary Fig. 33). Completing the full device architecture on microdomain underlayers prepared with 2PACz microdomains of 30–50 μm in diameter (Supplementary Fig. 34), enables solar-driven OWS under unbiased, photocatalytic operation (Supplementary Fig. 35). The system produced 0.18 μmol h−1 cm−2 of H2 (at a H2-to-O2 ratio of 2), corresponding to an estimated STH conversion efficiency of 0.01%. This performance aligns well with our observation of the STH performance of devices with controlled 100-μm domains. Selecting for larger droplet sizes in the millimetre range should, thereby, in the future enable the scalable fabrication of OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheets with higher performance.Overall, the photocatalytic operation of our OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheets confirms that molecular underlayer domain-dependent directional photogenerated charge extraction from the BHJ to the FTO substrate enables Z-scheme functionality with the same working principle as in inorganic nanoparticle-based photocatalyst sheets, but with a single, bifunctional light-absorbing layer. Our work thereby establishes a rational design strategy for an organic semiconductor photocatalyst sheet and demonstrates solar-driven OWS using a purely OS BHJ-based photocatalyst system. The underlayer microdomain approach using molecular functionalization and the understanding of the domain-size limitations presented in this work can serve as the basis for further development of more efficient and stable OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheets. Lastly, the development of our spray-deposition method for microdomain underlayer preparation additionally highlights the accessibility and scalability of our device architecture.Limitations of demonstrated BHJ photocatalyst sheetUtilizing OS BHJ systems for solar-driven OWS offers great potential, mostly due to their superior light absorption ability. In an ideal case, the OS BHJ photocatalyst sheet in this study can achieve 11.1% STH conversion efficiency under AM1.5 G illumination. This could be further improved to 16‒17% by employing narrower-bandgap BHJ systems (see Supplementary Note 10 for details of theoretical maximum STH conversion efficiency estimation). However, several challenges remain. The recombination issue, originating from insufficient charge extraction in the BHJ at the underlayer domain boundaries, currently limits further miniaturization of the microdomains. General drawbacks of organic BHJ systems also remain, such as complex BHJ morphology and compatibility with inorganic HER/OER co-catalysts. Thus, future efforts will focus on advancing the practical viability of this scalable photocatalyst sheet by incorporating narrow-bandgap acceptors with low molecular diffusion rates into the BHJ system. Such acceptors, which are widely used in high-performance organic photovoltaics25,51, could increase the maximum achievable STH conversion efficiency while improving the morphological stability of the BHJ. Further improvements in CSC engineering, through the development of CSC molecules or advanced micropatterning techniques, could enhance the driving force for charge extraction, particularly at HSC/ESC domain boundaries, thereby minimizing recombination. In parallel, improving the operational stability of the individual half-reactions will require the development of molecular catalysts and, in particular, deposition methods for OER co-catalyst overlayers with enhanced domain selectivity.ConclusionsIn summary, we have developed a rationally designed OS BHJ-based photocatalyst sheet for unassisted solar-driven water splitting through an underlayer engineering strategy that establishes a microdomain architecture, affording H2 and O2 production from a single light-absorbing layer for both the HER and the OER. The carefully chosen PBDTTTPD:PNDIHDT BHJ is capable of driving both half-reactions depending on the charge-selective substrate functionalization, with the 2PACz-based photocathode delivering a Jph of 4.1 mA cm‒2 at 0 VRHE for the HER, while the NI-PA-based photoanode produced a Jph of 2.7 mA cm‒2 at 1.23 VRHE for the OER. To integrate the two separate photoelectrodes into a scalable photocatalyst sheet, we designed controlled CSC microdomains via PDMS stamp-based contact printing. The final FTO/2PACz:NI-PA/BHJ/Pt/PTAA/LIO photocatalyst sheet utilizing 1,000-μm 2PACz domains demonstrates both HER and OER in PEC measurements with a Jph of over 2 mA cm−2 at 0.1 VRHE and 1.4 mA cm−2 at 1.23 VRHE and a photocurrent crossover potential of 0.56 VRHE. Under bias-free photocatalytic operation under simulated 1-sun illumination, the photocatalyst sheet demonstrated OWS with a stabilized H2 production rate of 1.3 μmol h−1 cm−2, activity for over 2 h under continuous operation and an H2:O2 ratio of 2. Studying the effect of the underlayer microdomain size, we found that miniaturization below 1,000 μm leads to a drop in performance. This is most likely due to the increase in specific perimeter between differently functionalized FTO domains, increasing the proportion of micrometre-scale boundary regions of reduced charge extraction directionality. Utilizing a scalable spray-deposition technique for underlayer preparation, we have further demonstrated the broad accessibility of our device architecture, which can serve as a platform for further exploration of OSs as effective photo-absorbers for photocatalytic OWS.MethodsMaterialsChlorobenzene, chloroform, dichloromethane (DCM), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), Pd2(dba)3, P(o-tol)3, 2-aminoethyl phosphonic acid, PTAA, K2PtCl6, Na2SO4, Na2S2O8, LiOH·H2O and boric acid were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. Hexane was purchased from Merck/EMSURE. EtOH, isopropanol, MeOH, acetone, Na2SO3 and KH2PO4 were purchased from Acros. 1H,1H,2H,2H-Perfluorodecyltrichlorosilane was purchased from ABCR. Sylgard 184 was purchased from Dow Chemical Company. 1,8-Naphthalic anhydride, 2PACz and iridium(III) 2,4-pentanedionate were purchased from TCI. PNDIHDT polymer acceptor and all monomers used for polymerization were purchased from Ossila Ltd. All materials were used without further purification.Synthesis of PBDTTTPD(4,8-Bis(5-(2-ethylhexyl)thiophen-2-yl)benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]dithiophene-2,6-diyl)bis(trimethylstannane) (BDT-Sn, 100 mg), 1,3-dibromo-5-octyl-4H-thieno[3,4-c]pyrrole-4,6(5H)-dione (TPD-Br, 1 equiv.), Pd2(dba)3 (2 mol%) and P(o-tol)3 (8 mol%) were added to a round-bottom flask and then degassed. Unreacted monomers, catalysts and oligomer polymer chains were removed by successive Soxhlet purification with MeOH, acetone and hexane. The areas and depths of the microstructures were controlled by changing the lithography layouts and etching time, respectively. After stripping the photoresist with oxygen plasma, wafers were stored in a silane atmosphere of 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyltrichlorosilane for 12 h to form an anti-adhesive self-assembled monolayer on the surface. This was followed by heating at 140 °C for 10 min, washing with EtOH under sonication and drying. Using a vibrating mesh aerosol generator (H360-M05, TEKCELEO) at 100% power amplitude, a microdroplet mist of a 2 mM solution of 2PACz in EtOH was created. Large droplets and liquid condensate were caught in a reservoir at the bottom of the deposition setup. The micro-droplet-entrained mist was pushed onto a cleaned and activated FTO substrate placed on a hot plate (110 °C), using an Ar flow. When testing single electrodes in a three-electrode setup, an Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrode was used as the reference electrode and a Pt wire was employed as the counter electrode. The active area of the working electrode was 0.25 cm2. Simulated 1-sun illumination (AM 1.5 G, 100 mW cm−2) was generated by a 450 W xenon lamp and calibrated using a silicon photodiode (see detailed discussion of the lamp calibration procedure in Supplementary Information). For sacrificial reduction tests, 0.1 M NaBi buffer solution containing 0.5 M Na2S2O8 (pH 9) was used. Tests for sacrificial oxidation were performed in 0.5 M potassium phosphate (KPi) buffer containing 1.5 M Na2SO3 (pH 9). The scan rate for LSV data collection for sacrificial tests was 20 mV s−1. Water-splitting tests were performed in 0.5 M NaBi buffer electrolyte (pH 9) with an LSV scan rate of 10 mV s−1. The potential versus Ag/AgCl reference electrode was converted to RHE with the equation$${E}_{\mathrm{RHE}}={E}_{\mathrm{{Ag}/{AgCl}}}+0.059\times \mathrm{pH}+0.197$$
(1)
The STH conversion efficiency of the wired side-by-side PEC device under bias-free operation was calculated for the operational Jph after 30 min of photocurrent stabilization of the system, using the formula$${\mathrm {STH}}=\frac{1.23\,\left({\mathrm {V}}\right)\times {J}_{\mathrm{op}}\,\left(\mathrm{mA}\,{\mathrm{cm}}^{-2}\right)\times {\eta }_{\mathrm {F}}}{P\,({\mathrm {mW}}\,{\mathrm{cm}}^{-2})}$$
(2)
where Jop is the Jph under operation (0.1 mA cm−2), ηF is the Faradaic efficiency (100%) and P is the power of the incident light (100 mW cm−2).Photocatalyst testingH2 and O2 evolution rates were measured using a purge reactor with direct flow into the sample loop of a GC (Supplementary Fig. 24). Devices were placed inside a 20 ml glass vial containing 20 ml of 0.5 M NaBi buffer electrolyte (pH 9), closed with a septum cap and further sealed with polytetrafluoroethylene tape to prevent any leaks. The reactor was purged with N2 at a flow rate of 6 ml min−1 before and during illumination. Before illumination, the reactor was purged for at least 1 h in the dark until a stable O2 peak was observed using the GC. Subsequently, the device was illuminated with simulated 1-sun illumination (AM 1.5G, 100 mW cm−2), generated by a 500 W xenon lamp that was calibrated using a silicon photodiode. A Nexis GC-2030 (Shimadzu) fitted with a barrier discharge ionization detector and customized with an automated injection system (Chemlys SAS) was used to quantify the amount of H2 and O2 evolved, with injections from the sample loop every 5 min. Calibration for H2 and O2 evolution rates was conducted using Pt wires as working and counter electrodes. The STH conversion efficiency of photocatalytic systems was estimated using the following equation$$\mathrm{STH}=\frac{{{\rm{H}}}_{2}\,\mathrm{production}\,\mathrm{rate}\,({\mathrm{mmol}}\,{\rm{s}}^{-1})\times 237,200\,({{\rm{J}}}\,{\mathrm{mol}}^{-1})}{P\,({\mathrm{mW}}\,{\mathrm{cm}}^{-2})\times \mathrm{Area}\,({\mathrm{cm}}^{2})}$$
(3)
where P is the power of the incident light (100 mW cm−2).CharacterizationUV–visible absorption spectra were obtained using a UV–visible–near-infrared spectrophotometer (UV-3600, Shimadzu). DFT calculations using the Gaussian 09 package with the B3LYP/6-31G basis set were performed to estimate the dipole moments of 2PACz and NI-PA. UPS measurements were performed with an Axis Supra (Kratos Analytical) using 21.22 eV photons from a He I UV source. The pass energy was set to 10 eV and the samples were electrically grounded to limit charging effects. 1H NMR spectra were measured using a 400 MHz spectrometer (Bruker III HD 400). AFM and KPFM were measured with a Cypher S (Asylum Research) equipped with a Pt-coated cantilever (Olympus AC240TM). Line scan profiles were obtained with a 20-point line width. Top-view and cross-sectional SEM images were acquired using a Zeiss Merlin FE-SEM equipped with a Gemini II column, using either an annular secondary electron detector (in-lens) or a high-energy secondary electron (HE-SE2) detector. The electron high-tension was set to 2 kV, the probe current was set to 70 pA and the working distance was 3 mm. TEM samples were prepared by drop-casting dilute solutions of particles onto TEM grids (~3 nm amorphous carbon on 400 mesh copper grid, Ted Pella Inc.), followed by drying in vacuum at 60 °C for at least 4 h. TEM images were acquired with a Thermo Fisher Scientific Talos F220S microscope operated at 200 kV using a Ceta camera. BHJ layer thickness measurements were performed with a profilometer (Bruker, DektakXT).
